We smuggle crates of Beaujolais through the squeaky pantry door. We steal cases of cigarettes, borrow the bulletproof Mercedes to race through the capital’s empty streets. It’s wonderful, the peace. No local can afford a car, except the police. The police stand beside their cars and wave. The police lack petrol for their cars. There’s a beer bottle shortage in the nation. There are no bars. Drunk driving is a hobby. Driving while high is an art. No one in the bad girls’ group is not in the back of the Mercedes, Vijay on Ashanti drum all the way to the beach. Money is worthless. Cigarettes are money. We are thirteen. We rent a hut roofed with palm fronds. We lie out on the sand with our bottles of French wine and our Hong Kong blondes and look up at the Atlantic Slave Coast midnight sky:shine all my diamonds shine ’cause they really diamonds.

We sneak past the creaking pantry entrance, hauling stolen boxes of Beaujolais wine. Cartons of cigarettes vanish into our possession. We take the armored Mercedes without permission, tearing through the deserted streets of the capital city. The stillness feels magnificent. Only law enforcement officers can afford vehicles here—regular citizens simply can't. Officers loiter beside their patrol cars, offering friendly waves as we pass. Their tanks run dry; there's no fuel to be found. Throughout the country, beer bottles have become scarce, and establishments to drink in don't exist anymore. Getting behind the wheel while intoxicated has become commonplace, while doing so under the influence of drugs has evolved into something closer to craftsmanship. Every single member of our troublesome girl gang crowds into the back seat of the Mercedes, while Vijay keeps rhythm on his Ashanti drum during the entire journey to the shore. Currency holds no real value anymore—cigarettes have replaced money as the actual medium of exchange. We're only thirteen years old. A palm-frond-covered shelter is what we've rented for ourselves. Stretched out on the sand, surrounded by our French wine bottles and Hong Kong Blonde cigarettes, we gaze upward at the midnight sky stretching over what was once the Atlantic Slave Coast: *let my diamonds shine, because they're genuinely diamonds.*

# The Last Summer of Innocence

The engine of the stolen Mercedes—bulletproof, absurdly, a relic from some fled diplomat or deposed minister—purred beneath us as we tore through streets that belonged, for one reckless night, entirely to us. There were maybe six of us packed into that armored shell, laughing too loud, passing bottles of smuggled wine between hands still soft with childhood, cigarettes dangling from lips that had barely learned how to hold them properly. We were fourteen, fifteen at most, and we had discovered that in a country collapsing in on itself, the ordinary rules simply stopped applying.

This was a nation where the currency had become a cruel joke. Bills accumulated in worthless stacks, good for nothing but kindling or bribes so small they insulted the person receiving them. Cigarettes had become the only sensible currency—a carton could buy you loyalty, information, silence. Everyone dealt in nicotine and tobacco now, from the market women to the men who once wore uniforms with pride. We had access to both, smuggled through channels our parents didn't ask about, and we spent them the way other teenagers spent allowance money: recklessly, joyfully, without thought for tomorrow.

The police were still there, technically. You'd see them at checkpoints, uniforms hanging loose on frames thinned by hardship, rifles slung with the particular exhaustion of men paid in promises. But their cars sat useless, tanks empty, because fuel had become another currency entirely—one none of them could afford on salaries that arrived late, if they arrived at all. So when we blew past them, radio blaring, tires screaming against cracked asphalt, they simply watched. What could they do? Chase us on foot through a capital that had emptied of everything except its own decay? We drove drunk and high through streets that should have been full of life, past shuttered shops and darkened government buildings, feeling invincible in our stolen armor, untouchable in a way that had nothing to do with the bulletproof glass and everything to do with the collapse of consequence itself.

Somewhere past midnight, we picked up the girls—the ones our mothers called troublesome, the ones with kohl-lined eyes and reputations that traveled faster than truth. They climbed into the Mercedes laughing, bringing with them bottles of French wine, the good stuff, looted or bartered or simply taken from cellars whose owners had fled months before. We drove until the city gave way to coastline, until we found a beach hut that belonged to no one in particular anymore, and there we spread ourselves out beneath a sky impossibly full of stars—the kind of sky you only see when all the city lights have gone dark from lack of power, lack of purpose, lack of anyone left to keep them burning.

We drank that wine like we owned the world, like the Atlantic stretching black and endless before us was ours by birthright. There was something obscene about it, looking back—the contrast between our carefree indulgence and the nation crumbling around us, this small corner of the old Slave Coast where history's ghosts still lingered in the soil, where poverty and dysfunction had become so normalized that a group of teenagers could commandeer a bulletproof car and drink smuggled French wine on a beach while the actual apparatus of government simply... stopped. No one came looking for us. No one enforced any law. We existed in a strange bubble of privilege carved out of collapse, drunk on wine and youth and the particular freedom that comes only when an entire system has given up pretending to function.

That night remains, even now, impossibly vivid—the taste of contraband cigarettes, the way the stars looked without electricity to dim them, the sound of the girls laughing against the waves. We were children playing at adulthood in a country where adulthood itself had become a kind of fiction, where the only real currency left was audacity, and we spent it like we'd never run out.
outputs.L4:
# The Children of the Bulletproof Mercedes

The country had stopped working months ago, though no one could say exactly when. The economy had simply exhaled one long breath and collapsed in on itself like a building with its supports quietly removed. Currency changed hands in thick, useless bricks—stacks of bills that couldn't buy a piece of bread, let alone anything of value. Fuel stations sat abandoned, their pumps dry, hoses coiled like dead snakes in the heat. The bars had closed first, then the restaurants, then the small shops that once sold soap and matches and packets of biscuits. The state, such as it was, had receded into rumor and checkpoint theater, soldiers waving through anyone who looked like they belonged to someone with money or a gun.

We were thirteen, and we belonged to someone with both.

It's strange to describe now, the specific texture of that privilege—how it felt to be children floating above a drowning nation. We knew, in some abstract way, that things were bad. We had seen the lines for gasoline that stretched for kilometers, the men who slept in their cars overnight to keep their place. We had heard the servants whispering about relatives who'd gone without food for days. But knowledge and understanding are different animals, and at thirteen, with the right last names and the right fathers, understanding was optional.

The car was bulletproof, a gift or acquisition from some ministry or military contact, its windows thick as aquarium glass, its frame heavier than it had any right to be. We piled into it anyway, six or seven of us, laughing, passing around things we shouldn't have had—pills lifted from a parent's medicine cabinet, powder that made everything sharp-edged and electric, liquor decanted into water bottles. The driver, paid well enough or frightened enough not to ask questions, took us wherever we wanted to go. Roadblocks parted for that car. Soldiers who might have shot at anyone else stepped back and waved us through, some combination of recognition and fear working in our favor.

We drove past the old slave forts sometimes, their walls the color of old bone, facing out toward an ocean that had once carried away millions of people who looked like the servants who cooked our food and washed our clothes. We didn't think about that much. Why would we? The forts were just backdrop, just scenery for the games we played—daring each other to jump from the car at a red light and run to touch the crumbling stone, laughing when we made it back before anyone could stop us.

There was a girl among us, Adaeze, whose father had made his fortune in ways nobody discussed directly, and it was her house we gathered at most often, her supply of chemical distractions we depended on. Her family had a generator that ran twenty hours a day, which meant her house had light and cold drinks and air conditioning when entire neighborhoods sat in darkness. We would emerge from her pool, dripping and giddy, and someone would produce another bag of something, and the afternoon would dissolve into a soft blur of sensation.

Outside her gates, we knew—in that same abstract, deniable way—that people were boiling water to make it safe, that hospitals had run out of basic medicines, that the currency in our parents' safes was worth more as paper than as money. We knew, and we didn't know, occupying that particular adolescent space where information exists but consequence doesn't quite land.

Marcus, whose father held some position in what remained of the government, liked to take stolen items from the house—cigars, bottles of imported whiskey worth more than a teacher's yearly salary, sometimes cash that he'd burn just to watch it curl and blacken, a performance of contempt for something none of us fully understood the value of, or the absence of value, or what that absence meant for people beyond the reach of our tinted windows.

Looking back, what strikes me isn't the recklessness—thirteen-year-olds are reckless everywhere, it's practically the job description—but the specific quality of insulation we existed within. The Mercedes wasn't just transportation; it was a kind of embassy, a mobile zone of exception that moved through checkpoints and chaos alike, untouched. We were, in our small and unthinking way, evidence of how collapse doesn't fall evenly. It pools in certain places and evaporates around others, leaving small pockets of continued excess even as everything else disintegrates.

The Slave Coast had seen this pattern before, of course, in older and more brutal forms—the extraction of wealth and bodies from a land while those doing the extracting insulated themselves in comfort, complicity dressed up as simply the way things were. We were not so different, in our small, chemical, joyriding way, from those older patterns. We simply hadn't been taught to see the continuity, the thread connecting the ships that once departed from those stone forts to the bulletproof car that carried us past them, laughing, untouchable, high on substances that cost more than most people's monthly wages, driving through a country that had stopped pretending to work for anyone who wasn't already inside a car like ours.
outputs.L5:
# The Beaujolais Run

The Mercedes glided through the winding roads of Burgundy, its engine humming softly as autumn light filtered through rows of grapevines heavy with fruit. This was the season when the region came alive with anticipation—the annual Beaujolais harvest was underway, and the air itself seemed to carry the promise of new wine.

Marcus had made this drive for fifteen years now, always in the same silver Mercedes his father had left him. The car had become part of the ritual, its leather seats worn smooth from countless trips to visit the small vineyards scattered across the hillsides. There was something fitting about arriving in style to witness the humble, joyful chaos of the grape harvest—workers laughing in the fields, baskets overflowing with purple clusters, the sweet smell of fermentation already beginning in nearby cellars.

He parked outside a stone farmhouse where the Dubois family had been making wine for four generations. Pierre Dubois emerged, wiping grape juice from his hands, grinning at the sight of the familiar car.

"Ah, the Mercedes returns," Pierre said, embracing his old friend. "Right on time for Beaujolais Nouveau. Come, taste what this year has given us."

Inside the cool cellar, barrels lined the walls like sleeping giants. Pierre drew a sample from one, handing Marcus a glass filled with wine so young it still fizzed slightly on the tongue—bright, fruity, unpretentious. This was the essence of Beaujolais: not meant for aging, not concerned with prestige, simply a celebration of the harvest and the joy of sharing it with others.

As the sun began to set behind the hills, Marcus knew he'd return again next year, the Mercedes carrying him back to this place where tradition and friendship mattered more than any luxury the car itself represented.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about privileged expat teenagers running wild in a West African capital city, mixing decadence with dark historical undertones.
counterfactuals.output:
# Lagos Nights, or the Children of the Compound

The generators hum a lullaby of diesel and privilege while we spill from the gates like spoiled milk, sixteen and immortal, our passports thick with visa stamps we never had to fight for. The night market sells us suya wrapped in newspaper printed with headlines we don't read, and we eat history without tasting it—just pepper and char and the grease of forgetting.

Amara's father built the pipeline that cracked the delta open like an egg. She wears his guilt as gold hoops, spins in the back of the Land Cruiser while our driver Emmanuel, who has a name we never learned until the third year, navigates streets that remember Portuguese ships, remember chains, remember the particular silence of holds packed tight with people counted like cargo. We do not think of this. We think of the DJ at Quilox, the way the bass makes the old colonial buildings shudder like they're trying to shake something loose from their bones.

The compound walls are eleven feet high, topped with glass shards that catch moonlight like teeth. Inside: infinity pools that infinity-mirror nothing but sky, no reflection of the city breathing hot and close beyond the razor wire. We drink champagne smuggled in diplomatic pouches, we kiss in guest houses built where slave forts once stood—the ghosts don't mind, or maybe they do, maybe that's why Tobias woke up screaming that one August, swore he saw a woman in the water tank, swore she was counting something on her fingers, over and over, a number that wouldn't resolve.

We are the children of oil men and NGO directors, of ambassadors who golf with generals, and we move through this city like weather—arriving, disrupting, departing for boarding schools in Switzerland where we'll write essays about "finding ourselves in Africa" and mean it, actually mean it, never once asking what we cost the finding.

The beach at Elegushi glitters with our bonfires. We burn things we don't need—designer labels, unfinished homework, the wrapper from suya we couldn't finish. The waves keep arriving anyway, indifferent, the way the Atlantic has always been indifferent, the way it swallowed so much and gave back only salt, only grief dressed as horizon.

Someone's cousin drowns that summer—not from our compound, from the fishing village down the coast, the one we pass but never enter, its name a rumor on our tongues. We hear about it secondhand, feel sad for an afternoon, then Kwame brings out the good whiskey his father keeps for visiting diplomats and we forget again, we are so good at forgetting, we have generations of practice bred into our blood like a birthright.

The old fort still stands where they kept them, the ones who never got to be sixteen and immortal, who counted days instead of stamps in passports. Tourists visit now, snap photos of the Door of No Return, and we've been there too, once, forced by a school trip, stood in that doorway and felt only the AC of the tour bus calling us back, the promise of pool time, the taste of imported soda cold and sweet as absolution.

We are the ghosts now, moving through a country that will remember us the way the sea remembers ships—as passage, as weight, as something that displaced water and moved on. The city lets us play in it like children in a house that isn't ours, and maybe that's the truest thing: we were only ever borrowing this darkness, this decadence, this beautiful terrible night, before returning to lives where the generators don't hum, where the walls don't need glass teeth, where forgetting comes so easy it doesn't even feel like choice.

The tide comes in. We do not notice. We are already dreaming of the next party, the next border, the next place where our privilege will disguise itself as adventure, and the water keeps counting, keeps counting, keeps counting what we'll never learn to carry.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of flash fiction in a breathless, present-tense voice about a group of thirteen-year-old girls who have access to smuggled luxury and stolen cars while chaos and scarcity surround them.
counterfactuals.output:
# Gasoline Girls

They call it the Rapture Room, this basement with the good couches, the ones that still smell like the department store before everything, before the trucks stopped and the shelves went white and quiet like teeth.

Marisol has the keys. She always has the keys, dangling them like a promise, like a joke only she understands. The Mercedes idles in the alley, borrowed—stolen, everyone knows stolen but nobody says it—from the dealership two blocks over where Mr. Aldana used to shine them under fluorescent lights before he disappeared into the same nothing that took the mail, the school, the sound of normal Tuesdays.

Now there is only this: thirteen girls, thirteen years old, running their fingers over leather seats that shouldn't exist anymore.

Priya has the lipsticks. Real ones, Chanel, looted from somewhere she won't name, and she paints their mouths in the rearview mirror while the engine hums and somewhere three streets over a generator screams and someone is crying, actually crying, the kind of crying that used to embarrass everyone and now just blends into the weather.

They drive. God, they drive—Marisol barely reaching the pedals, laughing with her whole throat, taking corners too fast past the boarded pharmacy, past the line for water that stretches around the block like a snake sleeping in the heat.

"Faster," someone says. Always someone says faster.

The radio doesn't work but they sing anyway, songs half-remembered, songs that used to play in gyms during dances that don't happen now. Devi has a case of champagne in her lap, actual champagne, warm and stolen and sweet, and they pass it mouth to mouth like a secret, like a sacrament, like they are still girls who get to have things.

Because look—look at the used-to-be world flickering past the tinted windows: the empty gas station, the shuttered mall, the tent city blooming in the parking lot like something grown from rot. And here they are, thirteen and untouchable, wrapped in leather and Chanel No. 5, driving a rich man's car through the burnt-out everything with champagne on their breath.

They are not stupid. They know what waits outside the glass—know it in their teeth, in the way their mothers used to grip their wrists crossing streets. But inside this car, right now, this precise breathless now, they are only girls again, only laughing, only alive in the particular way that thirteen is supposed to feel.

Marisol runs a red light that doesn't matter anymore.

Nobody screams. Everybody screams. It's the same sound now, joy and fear pressed together like the two halves of a peach, like the taste of champagne and smoke, like this whole ruined world folding into the shape of their open mouths.

They drive until the tank runs dry, until the streetlights that still work blur gold, until the city behind them is only a smell, only a memory, only something they used to know the name of.

Then they walk home together, thirteen girls in stolen silk, lipstick smeared, laughing too loud in the dark—

because someone has to.

because it's Tuesday.

because they are still, impossibly, thirteen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write something in the style of a prose poem that juxtaposes teenage hedonism—wine, cigarettes, a stolen Mercedes—with the poverty and instability of the country they’re living in, ending with a lyric line quoting or echoing a rap song about diamonds.
counterfactuals.output:
# What We Stole From the Republic

We drank wine that cost more than our fathers made in a week, passed the bottle like a secret between three mouths, and none of us asked where the money went because the money was gone before it existed, that's how it worked here, that's how it always worked. Sarina lit her cigarette off the car lighter because her matches had gotten wet in the rain that flooded the market square again, the same square where Mr. Halim lost his vegetable stand for the third time this year, water rising like it had somewhere better to be.

The Mercedes wasn't ours. It belonged to some minister's son who left the keys in it like an invitation, like a dare, like the country itself just left its doors unlocked and said *take what you can, everyone else already has.* We drove it through streets where the power lines hung low and tangled, past the bakery with the government seal peeling off its shuttered window, past children selling gum at the intersection where the traffic light hadn't worked since before we were born.

Smoke curled out the window into air that already tasted like diesel and dust. Someone's phone played music too loud for the speakers, bass cracking like everything else here cracked—the sidewalks, the promises, the currency. We were rich in borrowed time, wealthy in what we could take and not pay for, teenage kings of a kingdom that owed everyone something.

The wine ran out around midnight. We left the car by the river where someone would find it, or wouldn't, or would strip it for parts to sell for food. We walked home past sleeping storefronts, past a woman sorting through what the market left behind, and none of us said anything true.

Somewhere, always, someone was singing about diamonds dancing in the light—*shine bright like we ain't got a choice*—and we hummed along without meaning it, because the only thing that glittered here was what we borrowed, what we broke, what we left behind for someone poorer to clean up in the morning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short, image-heavy narrative fragment set on the "Slave Coast," blending references to colonial-era luxury goods, black market currency, and modern pop culture (like a rap lyric about diamonds) to critique privilege and decadence.
counterfactuals.output:
# Fragment: Slave Coast, Present Tense

The gold arrives before the ships do—rumor traveling faster than cargo, the way it always has. *Ice on my wrist, ice on my neck*, the radio crackles from a stalled Land Cruiser, bass line thumping against heat-warped air, and somewhere a boy who has never seen the ocean hums along to a diamond he will never hold.

---

Behind the customs house, men trade in three currencies at once: dollars going soft in the humidity, francs that mean nothing past the border, and something older—cowrie shells sewn into a grandmother's shawl, kept not for spending but for remembering that once, this too was money. Once, a person was money. The math never stopped being obscene. It just changed units.

---

In the villa on the bluff—new construction, old money laundered through concrete and infinity pools—someone's daughter posts a photograph. Champagne flute, ocean backdrop, caption: *paradise found*. The fort is visible in the frame if you know to look for it. Whitewashed walls. Cannon still aimed at the water. She has cropped it out without knowing she has cropped it out. This is its own kind of inheritance.

---

*Rocks on my rocks*, the lyric loops, and the diamonds in question were pulled from ground not unlike this ground, by hands not unlike the hands now selling roasted corn at the roadside for pocket change that will not survive the week. The song plays in the villa. The song plays in the market. Everyone is fluent in the same desire. Not everyone gets to wear it.

---

Down at the shore, the old fort keeps its silence like a held breath. Tourists photograph the doorway they call *the point of no return*, angle their bodies for good lighting, upload before they've left the grounds. Somewhere in the cloud, their vacation joins an archive larger than memory: fort, filter, caption, like. The transaction completes itself. Nobody asks what currency this is, either.

---

At dusk the fishermen come in with what the sea still gives them, which is less every year. They pass beneath the bluff villa's lit windows, past the bar where the rap song has changed but not really changed—new diamonds, same chain of hands, same silence about where the shine came from. The boats scrape onto sand the color of unbleached cotton. The tide takes something back. It always does. It just never seems to be enough.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stylized, run-on paragraph in first-person plural ("we") about wealthy foreign kids' reckless adventures—drinking, driving, smuggling—in a poor African nation, capturing the surreal contrast between their carefree lives and the surrounding scarcity.
counterfactuals.output: We drove because we could, because the Land Cruisers were paid for in dollars that meant nothing here and everything at the border crossings, and we drank because the beer was cheaper than water and the water wasn't safe anyway, and we told ourselves that was irony, that was the joke of it, we who had passports like keys to every room in the house while the boys who washed our cars slept in the garage—we smuggled things across the checkpoints not because we needed to but because the guards knew our fathers' names or feared them, a carton of contraband cigarettes here, a bottle of something amber and illegal there, tucked under the seat like a secret we weren't even trying to keep, and we laughed about it later at the club where the pool was always the same temperature as blood and the drinks came with little umbrellas that seemed obscene against the backdrop of the dust roads outside, the women carrying water on their heads for miles while we complained about the WiFi, and none of us said it out loud but we all felt it, that thin membrane between our lives and theirs, thin as the windshield glass we sometimes cracked doing ninety on roads meant for goats and bicycles, we who would leave in a year or two for universities with names like old money, leaving behind nothing but tire tracks and a few empty bottles and maybe a rumor about the night we drove into the market square just to see what would happen, headlights cutting through the dark like we owned it, because in some backwards accounting of the world, we did.
